question: The office building's solid external walls are "STB 25.0 WD 12.0" and "STB 20.0 WD 12.0". Read their layer order from the model and explain what kind of external wall construction this is, why the designer added the 120 mm layer, and what the outer surface of such a wall needs.
answer: Both are single-leaf reinforced-concrete walls with an external thermal insulation system (ETICS): the layer list starts on the outside with 120 mm hard insulation ("Wärmedämmung - Hart"), then 250 mm (or 200 mm) in-situ concrete, and in the 200 mm type a 50 mm gypsum lining on the room side (total 370 mm). The insulation is required because solid concrete may serve as an external wall only with an additional insulation layer — single-leaf walls with added (external or internal) insulation are the usual alternative to monolithic high-insulation masonry. Placing it outside keeps the concrete on the warm side. The insulation face is not left exposed: on the external side of insulation layers there is a risk of cracking (heat build-up, substrate with poor shear strength), so a mesh-reinforced mineral (or plastic-modified) render is used there.

question: Below the façade cladding the model continues the insulation with separate elements: "WD hart 200" walls around the plinth (−0.82 to 0.00 m) and around the basement (−3.67 to −0.37 m), and "WD 200 hart" slabs under the basement base slab and under the ground floor outside the basement. What is the designer trying to achieve with these elements, and what would happen if they were omitted?
answer: They keep a continuous 200 mm insulation envelope around the heated volume: façade insulation (200 mm mineral wool) runs down to ground level, the plinth and the reinforced-concrete basement walls get 200 mm hard (pressure-resistant) insulation on the outside, and the 300 mm base slab and the ground floor over the unexcavated part sit on 200 mm hard insulation. Good thermal insulation needs not only well-insulated components but proper connections between them. Without these pieces the bare concrete basement walls and slabs (concrete external parts need added insulation anyway) would be thermal bridges — areas with much lower insulation than the 200 mm-insulated surroundings, with heat loss and cold, condensation-prone inner surfaces. In a highly insulated envelope like this one (U ≈ 0.13–0.15 W/m²K), such bridges have proportionally worse consequences.

question: The four roof areas over the top offices are slabs "Basisdach:Titanzink - Eindeckung" (timber boarding + bitumen, titanium-zinc covering), modelled with PitchAngle 0. Would standard design guidance accept this roof geometry and build-up for a heated office building at concept stage?
answer: No, on two counts. (1) Fall: the roof is exactly flat (0°, 0 %). Flat roofs should have at least 2 % slope, and because of flatness tolerances and deflection Neufert recommends ≥ 5 % (3°); a roof with no fall is only an exceptional special construction — and a metal sheet covering is normally laid on a pitch. (2) Thermal envelope: the 80 mm package contains only timber boarding and bitumen, no insulation and no vapour barrier, so it is neither a warm roof (structure, vapour barrier, insulation and waterproofing as one composite) nor a cold roof. question: The flat part of the top roof is "Basic Roof:Flachdachaufbau begrünt 320" (a green roof, U 0.128 W/m²K), modelled perfectly level. Its constituents, listed outside to inside as in the model's other types, are greening, fleece, hard insulation, bitumen membrane. What flat-roof type is this, and what is wrong with the way it is modelled for a planted roof?
answer: With the insulation above the bitumen waterproofing, it is an upside-down (inverted) roof: waterproofing (doubling as vapour barrier) directly on the structure, insulation loosely laid on top — which must therefore be closed-cell, pressure-resistant insulation, consistent with "Dämmung - hart" — and the planting acting as ballast instead of gravel. The problem is the fall: the roof is modelled at 0°. Planted flat roofs should have a maximum slope of 2–3 %, and flat roofs in general at least 2 % (recommended 5 %), zero-fall being only an exceptional special construction. So the roof needs a fall of about 2 % (≈ 1.1°) — enough to drain, but not more than 3 % so the growing layer does not dry out.

question: The flat roof over part of the house is "Basic Roof:Warm Roof - Timber", modelled with PitchAngle 0. Check its layer sequence and its fall: is the build-up right, and where would the required fall come from?
answer: The layer sequence is correct: asphalt 20 mm and felt (waterproofing), 50 mm rigid insulation, a vapour retarder, 18 mm chipboard deck, 50 mm firrings and 200 mm timber joists (338 mm). Structure, vapour barrier, insulation and waterproofing form the composite of a non-ventilated warm roof, and the vapour retarder lies on the warm side directly under the insulation, where a vapour barrier has to be to avoid condensation behind the vapour-tight waterproofing (the book places it under the insulation in pitched roofs for the same reason). The geometry, however, is modelled with 0° (PitchAngle 0, top at +2.54 m throughout), while flat roofs should have at least 2 % fall (5 % recommended). The 50 mm firring layer is where the fall belongs (tapered firrings on the joists); over the ≈ 13 m long roof 2 % needs ≈ 0.26 m, so 50 mm firrings alone would give only ≈ 0.4 % unless the joists are also laid to falls.

question: The FZK house has a 30° gable roof over a habitable 74.5 m² attic room, but the roof is modelled only as two 200 mm "Solid" slabs (ThermalTransmittance 0.3). For a habitable attic under a pitched roof, where would the thermal insulation and the vapour barrier normally go, and should the roof be built as a ventilated or an unventilated construction?
answer: The insulation (usually mineral wool) goes between and under the rafters, with the vapour barrier on the room side and battens fixed to the rafters. An unventilated construction is the usual choice: a ventilated roof needs extra rafter depth and only works with a correctly installed vapour barrier and functioning roof ventilation, so the industry commonly prefers unventilated roofs. None of these layers is modelled: the roof is a single homogeneous 200 mm slab with a stored U-value of 0.3, so the build-up has to be added before the envelope can be checked.

Their constituents, outside to inside, are: roof tiles, air layer, timber, soft insulation, air layer, timber. Is this a ventilated or a non-ventilated pitched-roof construction, and what layer does it then rely on that the model does not show?
answer: Non-ventilated. The air layer directly under the tiles is the covering's batten space, which both roof types have; a ventilated roof would need an additional ventilation gap between the underlay (here the outer timber boarding) and the insulation, and there is none — the insulation lies directly under the boarding. The second air layer is on the room side of the insulation, behind the inner timber lining, i.e. a service void, not a ventilation path. This unventilated build-up is the one the industry prefers (ventilated roofs need extra rafter depth and work only with a correct vapour barrier and functioning ventilation), but it depends on an airtight vapour barrier on the room side under the insulation, sealed at all joints and penetrations — no such constituent is in the model.

question: Each upper floor of this building holds two flats, one in the west wing and one in the east wing. The only room-to-room contact between them is at the north end, where Utility room 27 (west) and Utility room 35 (east) on the First Floor share a single wall. Identify that wall. Given the building's regulatory class, what fire performance must it have, and does its geometry meet the requirement?
answer: The shared wall is "STB 15.0 - Sichtbeton" (0RgKgXPa5AqeGvHba2KWCC), 150 mm of exposed reinforced concrete, at x −3.09 to −2.94 m. The building has 6 flats (2 per floor) and about 1401 m² of spaces, so by the book's gloss for building classes 3–5 ("more than two flats or a usable area of 400 m²", given in brackets in its rubbish-storage rule) it is in class 3–5. A wall between two residential units must have the fire resistance of the storey's load-bearing components. Here those are reinforced concrete: STB 30.0 outer walls, STB 15.0 load-bearing cross walls and an STB 20.0 slab. A 150 mm solid concrete wall is non-combustible and as massive as the load-bearing 150 mm walls. Assuming the same concrete class and cover as those walls, it reaches the same fire resistance even though it is flagged LoadBearing = False. It also has to run up to the structural slab. It goes from 3.40 m to 6.60 m, which is exactly the underside of the 200 mm Second Floor slab (6.60–6.80 m). So it complies.

question: This single-family house combines cast concrete walls ("CL_W1", "Retaining - 300mm Concrete") with timber construction: structural timber insulated panels finished with timber cladding ("Wall - Timber Clad"), timber-stud partitions and a concrete-clad SIP wall. If it were built under the German model building regulations, would its fire-protection class allow this timber construction and the timber façade cladding? Explain.
answer: Yes. The house is one dwelling with about 279 m² of rooms (Level 1 177.2 m², Level 2 101.7 m²). That is fewer than three flats and less than 400 m², so by the book's gloss for classes 3–5 ("more than two flats or a usable area of 400 m²", a bracket in its rubbish-storage rule) it falls below class 3, i.e. class 1–2. In classes 1–2, load-bearing and bracing walls only need to be fire-retarding, a level timber-panel and timber-stud walls can reach. Non-load-bearing external walls need not be non-combustible in classes 1–3. External wall claddings, including insulation and support construction, must in general be flame-resistant, which untreated timber cladding is not; but classes 1 and 2 are the exception: there cladding of normally flammable material, here the 22 mm timber cladding over the SIP walls, is permissible as long as the spread of fire to neighbouring buildings is effectively prevented. The model gives no plot boundaries, so that condition (distance or a non-combustible wall towards a neighbour) has to be checked on the site plan. The solid concrete walls are well above the requirement anyway.

question: This office building has a full basement ("Keller", −3.00 m) under four storeys. The basement walls are 300 mm and 200 mm Kalksandstein (calcium-silicate) masonry, and the ground-floor slab above it is 300 mm "Stahlbeton". Determine the building's class from the model. What fire performance does that class require of the basement walls and of the slab over the basement, and are the chosen constructions appropriate?
answer: The spaces add up to 1939.4 m², about 430 m² per storey, so it is clearly over the 400 m² usable area that the book (in a bracket in its rubbish-storage rule) equates with building classes 3–5; on that gloss it is in class 3–5. In cellars, load-bearing and bracing walls and columns must then be fireproof (the class 1–2 relief to fire-retarding does not apply), and the slab over the cellar must be fireproof; the book's exceptions to the slab rule (classes 1 and 2, ceilings above roof spaces, slabs within dwellings) do not cover a class 3–5 office basement. The basement walls are solid calcium-silicate masonry, 300 mm outside and 200 mm inside, plastered on both faces. They are non-combustible, massive walls, the kind normally classified fireproof, though the model carries no fire rating, so this is an assumption. The 300 mm solid reinforced-concrete slab over the basement (Decke-001 at −0.30…0.00 m) is a solid slab. Neufert says such slabs have enough fire resistance without additional protection under certain conditions (mainly concrete cover). So both constructions are appropriate. The rating still has to be shown, and the model's Pset_WallCommon has no FireRating.

question: The external walls of this office building ("Kalksandstein … 300", 54 walls) are modelled as one 300 mm layer of calcium-silicate masonry, plastered on both faces. Judge this single-material external wall against the usual design guidance on external wall construction, and say what a designer would add or change.
answer: As modelled, the wall is not a viable heated external wall. It is a single-leaf wall: ArchiCAD reports structure type "Einfach", insulation layer thickness 0.0 and air layer thickness 0.0, and the only material is Kalksandstein 300 mm, plastered both sides. Neufert notes that single-leaf external walls are simple in building-physics terms, but under current thermal insulation requirements they can only be built from materials with high thermal insulation value, such as aerated blocks, with insulating mortars and plasters. Calcium-silicate masonry is a dense, load-bearing unit, the opposite of an insulating block. So either an insulation layer is added (an external insulation system or a cavity/core-insulated two-leaf wall), or the wall is changed to an insulating masonry unit, which would usually need more thickness than 300 mm. At early design stage, this adds roughly 100–200 mm to the wall line all round the 42 × 14 m footprint.

question: The FZK house's external walls are "Leichtbeton … 300" and its internal walls "Leichtbeton … 240", each a single homogeneous material layer with no insulation layer modelled. Why would a designer choose a single-leaf lightweight-concrete external wall, and why is it thicker than the internal walls?
answer: It is a single-leaf external wall. Neufert accepts this form, and it is simple in building-physics terms, but only if the wall material itself insulates well (aerated blocks are his example) and is laid with insulating mortars and plasters. Lightweight concrete (Leichtbeton) is that kind of porous, insulating masonry, so the 300 mm external wall can be both structure and insulation without a separate layer or a second leaf. The extra 60 mm over the 240 mm internal walls is for insulation: the internal walls only have to carry loads and separate rooms, while the external wall also carries the thermal duty, and for a homogeneous wall that means more thickness. This assumes the Leichtbeton is an insulating grade. If it were a dense grade, the wall would need additional insulation like any other single-leaf wall.

question: Around the building, the model places separate wall elements just outside the structural walls: "WD 200 + Luft 40 + Bekleidung 12" (rock wool, air gap, fibre-cement board) outside the "Leichtbetonmauerwerk 250" façade walls, and "WD hart 200" outside the "STB 300" basement walls and under the basement slab. What construction principle is the designer following, and why is it needed for these particular structural walls?
answer: The designer is wrapping the structure in a continuous outer insulation layer, so the structural walls stay on the warm side. Above ground, the 250 mm lightweight-concrete masonry gets 200 mm rock wool, a 40 mm air gap and 12 mm fibre-cement cladding: a back-ventilated façade, with U = 0.151 W/m²K stored on the type. Below ground, the 300 mm reinforced-concrete basement walls and the basement slab get 200 mm hard insulation (perimeter insulation). Neufert gives the reasons. Under current insulation requirements, single-leaf external walls can only be built from materials of high insulation value, which 250 mm masonry alone is unlikely to provide (the model gives no conductivity, so this is an assumption); single-leaf walls with additional insulation layers are therefore the common alternative. And solid concrete walls may be used as external walls only with an additional thermal insulation layer. Putting the insulation outside keeps the mass of the concrete and masonry inside the thermal envelope. It also lets the insulation run unbroken past the slab edges and columns.

question: On OG1, "Corridor west" (≈1.58 m wide, ≈21.3 m long) leads from the individual offices and WCs to the "Staircase core (west)". List the wall types that form its two sides. Assuming the corridor serves as an escape route, what fire performance must those side walls have, and which wall needs the most attention?
answer: The side walls of an escape-route corridor must be at least fire-retarding (F 30). The east side is "STB 30.0" reinforced concrete throughout (y −21.10…0.45). The west side is, from south to north: the "STB 25.0" stair-core walls (y −20.80…−13.89), the "STB 20.0" WC wall (y −13.64…−7.84), and then "GK 12.5" between the corridor and Individual offices 1 and 2 (y −7.84…0.50). The concrete walls are non-combustible solid walls, far beyond F 30. The one to watch is the GK 12.5: a 125 mm stud partition of gypsum board with hard insulation between. Non-load-bearing separating walls can be built as stud partitions of various qualities, so it can be detailed to F 30. But it has to be a rated system, and it runs the full storey height (3.70–7.10 m, up to the STB 30.0 slab at 7.10–7.40 m). The model stores no FireRating on any wall. The only rated element on the corridor is the EI 30 door to the WC. There is no glazing in the corridor walls, so no G-glazing sill question arises. (If the whole floor counted as one small use unit, the corridor might be exempt from escape-route rules. The verdict above assumes it is a required corridor.)

question: For the six ground-floor rooms, the model gives both a GrossFloorArea and a NetFloorArea (e.g. Wohnen 25.99 / 25.21 m², Küche 16.31 / 16.31 m²). The walls are modelled as bare "Leichtbeton" with no plaster layer. Which of the two values matches how room areas are measured for a dwelling's housing area, and is the model consistent about it?
answer: NetFloorArea is the right value, but the kitchen is inconsistent. Under the housing-area regulation Neufert summarises, a room's floor area is the clear space between building components, measured from the face of their cladding (plaster, linings), so a figure taken to the raw wall overstates it. Each room's GrossFloorArea equals its space solid, which runs between the raw Leichtbeton wall faces (Wohnen 7.01 × 3.71 m ≈ 25.99 m²). For five rooms, NetFloorArea is exactly 97 % of that: Flur 11.53 → 11.19, Buero 12.99 → 12.60, Bad 12.50 → 12.13, Schlafzimmer 22.07 → 21.41, Wohnen 25.99 → 25.21 m². This is a flat 3 % deduction, evidently for the wall finishes the model does not show. The Küche gets no deduction (16.31 m² for both values), so it is measured to the raw walls. With the same 3 % it would be ≈ 15.82 m², and the ground floor would total ≈ 98.34 m² instead of the listed 98.83 m² (101.39 m² raw).

question: Using DIN 277 terms, derive three figures for the FZK house: the gross floor area of the whole house, the constructional floor area of its ground floor, and the net floor area of both levels together.
answer: Gross floor area ≈ 240 m², ground-floor constructional area ≈ 18.6 m², net floor area ≈ 192.7 m². Gross floor area is measured over the external dimensions of the enclosing elements at floor height. Both the Erdgeschoss and the Dachgeschoss lie within the 12.00 × 10.00 m outer wall faces, so it is 2 × 120.0 = 240.0 m². Net floor area is the area between the building elements. On the ground floor, the six room solids, which run between the raw wall faces, add up to 101.4 m². In the attic, the Galerie's 11.40 × 9.40 = 107.16 m² minus the 15.80 m² stair void (a cut-out, not floor) gives ≈ 91.4 m². Together that is ≈ 192.7 m², about 80 % of the gross floor area. Constructional floor area is the plan area of the walls themselves. On the ground floor it is 120.0 − 101.4 ≈ 18.6 m², which matches the 0.30 m outer ring (120.0 − 107.16 = 12.84 m²) plus ≈ 5.8 m² of 0.24 m inner walls. DIN 277 makes no height reduction, unlike the housing-area calculation, so the Galerie's low eaves zones count in full here.

question: Treat the modelled terrain "Gelaende" (≈18 × 16 m, extending 3.0 m beyond the house on every side) as the plot. How deep a setback area must the house keep free in front of its walls, does the plot provide it, and what plot coverage ratio does the house produce?
answer: 3 m on every side. The terrain gives exactly 3.0 m from the walls, but whether that suffices depends on the 0.5 m roof overhang (see below); the plot coverage ratio is ≈ 0.42. Under the model building regulations (MBO; state LBOs differ) the setback depth is 0.4 × H, but at least 3 m. H is the wall height from ground level to the intersection with the roof covering, plus one third of the height of a roof pitched ≤ 70°. Eaves walls: H ≈ 3.4 m + ⅓ × ≈ 2.9 m of roof ≈ 4.4 m, so 0.4 H ≈ 1.8 m. Even the gable walls taken at their full height to the ridge covering (+6.32 m) only need 0.4 × 6.32 ≈ 2.5 m. Both are below the 3 m minimum. For a detached one-family house with two storeys (building class 1–2, not more than three storeys), 3 m is sufficient in any case. The terrain runs from −3.0 to 15.0 m in x and from −3.0 to 13.0 m in y around the 0–12 × 0–10 m house, exactly 3.0 m on each side of the walls. Projecting elements such as cornices and roof overhangs are disregarded only if they take up altogether less than one third of the wall width, project at most 1.50 m and stay at least 2 m from the opposing boundary. The 0.5 m overhang meets the last two conditions (2.5 m from the terrain edge) but runs along the whole length of every wall, so it fails the one-third condition; measured from its edge, only 2.5 m of the required 3 m remain, 0.5 m short. Only if roof overhangs were taken as exempt regardless of these conditions would the house just comply. (This assumes the terrain edge is a boundary with private land: if it bordered a public road, green or water area, the setback area could extend onto it up to its centre, and the shortfall would disappear; the model shows no such neighbour.) Plot coverage = built area / plot area; the model has no garage, parking or underground facility to add, so built area = 120 m² and the ratio is 120 / 288 ≈ 0.42. The floor-area ratio is also ≈ 0.42 if only the ground floor counts as a full storey, or ≈ 0.83 if the attic did.

question: The two wings of the apartment building have hipped roofs. Their outer walls rise to +10.72 m and the roof covering reaches its ridge at +12.37 m. On the first and second floors, 3.0 m deep balconies (Balcony 1/3 and 2/6) run along about 29.7 m of the 32.85 m long west and east façades. How deep a setback area must be kept free in front of these long façades, and from where is it measured?
answer: About 4.5 m, measured from the outer edge of the balconies, so the clear strip reaches about 7.5 m from the façade walls. H is the wall height to the roof covering plus one third of the roof height, because the pitch is ≈ 31° (≤ 70°): 10.72 + (12.37 − 10.72) / 3 ≈ 11.27 m. 0.4 × 11.27 ≈ 4.5 m, which is above the 3 m minimum. This is the MBO rule; state LBOs differ. The 3 m concession for small buildings does not apply: it is limited to building classes 1–2, and a building with six flats is in classes 3–5 by the book's gloss (more than two flats). Projecting elements (cornices, roof overhangs and the like) are disregarded only if they take up altogether less than one third of the wall width, project no more than 1.50 m and stay at least 2 m from the opposing boundary. The balconies fail the first two tests: they run along ≈ 90 % of the façade length and are 3.0 m deep. So they count as part of the building (the 0.6 m eaves overhang lies within their depth and does not matter), and the 4.5 m strip starts at their outer edge (x −16.01 on the west, ≈ +10.0 on the east), about 7.5 m from the walls at x −13.01 and +6.99.

question: The office building has flat roofs. Its long west and east façades (x = −12.01 and +9.99 m) end in a parapet at +19.80 m. On the two 22 m wide end façades, the central 14 m (the two core blocks, x −8.01 to +5.99) rises flush with the façade to +24.30 m. If the plot lies in a commercial area, how deep must the setback areas in front of the long façades and the end façades be? How would they change in a residential or mixed area?
answer: In a commercial area: ≈ 4.0 m in front of the long façades and ≈ 4.9 m in front of the core part of the end façades (≈ 4.0 m for their outer 4 m parts). Elsewhere the depths double, to ≈ 7.9 m and ≈ 9.7 m. Under the model building regulations (MBO; the state LBOs differ) the setback depth is a factor × H, but at least 3 m. H is the wall height from ground level to the top of the wall, with no roof addition because the roofs are flat. Long façades: H = 19.80 m, so 0.2 H = 3.96 m in commercial and industrial areas and 0.4 H = 7.92 m elsewhere. Core sections: H = 24.30 m, so 0.2 H = 4.86 m and 0.4 H = 9.72 m. All of these exceed the 3 m minimum. The MBO concession that 3 m suffices for building classes 1–2 with not more than three overground storeys does not apply: the building has five storeys (EG–OG4). question: Count how many flats each of the two stairwells serves per floor and name the resulting access type. Judge it: what share of each floor does the stairwell take, and how many storeys could this type have if the lifts were left out?
answer: Each stairwell serves one flat per floor. Stairwell 1 serves only the west flats and Stairwell 2 only the east flats, with one front door per floor in each. The building is therefore two one-flat-per-floor stacks side by side, the "stacked terrace" or town-villa type. Neufert calls this type relatively uneconomic because access takes a high share of the floor area. Here the 20.81 m² stairwell serves one ≈ 154.8 m² flat (west ground floor: 18.07 + 4.33 + 38.45 + 36.53 + 26.42 + 8.18 + 13.37 + 9.42), i.e. ≈ 11.9 % of each floor (20.81 / 175.6). If one core served both flats of a floor (two flats per floor, the most common type), the share would fall to ≈ 6.3 % (20.81 / 330.4). Three flats per floor would give an even better balance of quality and cost. Without lifts, this type is generally limited to four floors, so the three storeys here do not need the lifts; lifts are only required above five full floors anyway. The lifts are a choice for comfort and accessibility, not a requirement.

question: The FZK house has seven spaces: Flur, Buero, Bad, Schlafzimmer, Wohnen, Küche and the attic Galerie. Does the dwelling contain the rooms that building regulations require in every house or flat? If one is missing, where could it go?
answer: No, the dwelling has no storeroom. Building regulations require every house or flat to have at least one kitchen or kitchenette, a bathroom, and a sufficiently large storeroom. The house has the Küche (16.3 m², open to the hall and the living room, but still a kitchen) and the Bad (12.1 m², the only sanitary room). No space serves as a storeroom: the other rooms are the bedroom, office, living room, hall and Galerie, and the model has no cellar or utility room. The natural place for one is the low eaves zone of the Galerie. Its clear height is only 0.67 m at the eaves walls, so these strips count for only half or nothing of the living area anyway. Alternatively, a walk-in store could be partitioned off the 1.74 m wide Flur at the cost of a narrower hall.

question: Fantasy office building 1 has flat roofs at two heights. The long east and west wings (outer curtain walls at x ≈ +10.0 m and x ≈ −12.05 m) end at a roof top of about 19.27 m. The two cross bars at the north and south ends (façades at y ≈ +10.6 m and y ≈ −21.1 m; their side walls above the wing roofs at x ≈ +5.62 m and −7.64 m) rise one storey higher, to about 24.16 m. Take ground level as the EG floor (0.00 m). How deep a strip must be kept free in front of each façade under the German model building regulations? What is the smallest rectangular plot that could hold the building with these strips? How does the answer change if the site is in a commercial area?
answer: About 7.7 m in front of the east and west façades and about 9.7 m in front of the north and south façades, so the plot must be at least about 37.5 × 51.1 m (≈1,914 m²). In a commercial area it is about 29.8 × 41.4 m (≈1,233 m²). The setback depth is 0.4 × H, but at least 3 m, where H is the wall height measured from ground level (here taken to the roof top, since no parapet is modelled). Wings: 0.4 × 19.27 = 7.71 m. Bars: 0.4 × 24.16 = 9.66 m. East/west: the wing façade governs. The wing strip reaches 10.02 + 7.71 = 17.73 m, while the bar side wall, set back to x 5.62, only reaches 5.62 + 9.66 = 15.28 m (west: −19.76 vs −17.30 m). North/south: the bar façades govern with 9.66 m (the wing ends need only 7.71 m). The MBO concession that 3 m suffices for classes 1–2 with not more than three overground storeys does not apply to this five-storey building (EG–OG4). The setback areas must lie on the plot itself; they may also lie on adjoining public traffic, green and water areas up to their centre, so the following minimum plot assumes no such neighbour. Plot: x −19.76…17.73 m = 37.5 m, y −30.77…20.28 m = 51.1 m. In a commercial area the depth is 0.2 × H, but at least 3 m: 3.85 m (wings) and 4.83 m (bars). That gives 22.07 + 2 × 3.85 = 29.8 m by 31.73 + 2 × 4.83 = 41.4 m.

question: In ac20 the ground surface is modelled by the site object "Gelaende 0815" (top at −0.15 m, extending x −8…50 m and y −11…27 m). Treat its outer edges as the plot boundary. The building has shallow curved roofs with a 1 m overhang. Does it keep the setback areas required by the German model building regulations on all four sides?
answer: Yes, comfortably. The setback depth is 0.4 × H, but at least 3 m. H runs from ground level to the top of the wall or its intersection with the roof covering. Roofs pitched at ≤ 70° add one third of their height. Long (eaves) façades: the south eaves wall (Wand-010) rises to 10.33 m, i.e. 10.48 m above the −0.15 m ground. The roof crest above it is 11.02 m, so the roof adds (11.02 − 10.33)/3 ≈ 0.23 m, giving H ≈ 10.7 m and a depth of ≈ 4.3 m. The available distance is 13 m (y 2 → −11), and also 13 m on the north side of the wings (y 14 → 27). Centre block, north side (y 16): the crest is 12.05 m, so H ≈ 10.48 + (12.05 − 10.33)/3 ≈ 11.05 m and the depth is ≈ 4.4 m. 11 m is available. Gable ends (x 0 and 42): counting the full gable wall (10.64 m) gives H ≈ 10.8 m and a depth of ≈ 4.3 m. 8 m is available on each side. Even in the worst case (full crest height, 12.2 m above ground, 0.4 × H ≈ 4.9 m, measured from the 1 m overhang because it runs along the whole eaves and so is not a negligible projection), every side keeps at least 8 − 1 − 4.9 ≈ 2.1 m in hand. In a commercial area the 3 m minimum would govern, which is easier still. The 3 m concession for classes 1–2 with at most three overground storeys is not needed (and would not apply to this four-storey office above ground). Treating the terrain edge as the boundary is conservative, since setback areas may also extend onto adjoining public traffic, green or water areas up to their centre.

question: Take the extent of the ac20 site object "Gelaende 0815" (x −8…50 m, y −11…27 m) as the plot. Work out the plot coverage ratio and the floor-area ratio that the building uses. State which storeys you count and why.
answer: Plot coverage ≈ 0.23 and floor-area ratio ≈ 0.70. The plot is 58 × 38 = 2,204 m². The footprint, from the external wall faces, is 42.0 × 12.0 = 504 m² plus the stair-hall projection of 6.0 × 2.0 = 12 m², so 516 m². The plot coverage ratio counts the building's plan area including garages, parking places and their access, subsidiary areas and underground facilities; the model has no garage or parking, so 516 / 2,204 ≈ 0.23. The basement lies within the same footprint, so it adds nothing. If the 2 m light wells along the long sides (≈ 132 m²) are counted as subsidiary built area, the ratio is ≈ 0.29. The floor-area ratio uses the external dimensions of all full floors: EG, 1. OG and 2. OG give 3 × 516 = 1,548 m², so 1,548 / 2,204 ≈ 0.70. The book does not define "full storey", so two assumptions are needed. The Keller is not counted: its ceiling (0.00 m) is only 0.15 m above the terrain (−0.15 m), so it is effectively underground. The Dachgeschoss is not counted: it is an attic whose rooms 402/403 have only ≈ 1.64 m clear height (z 9.00–10.64 m). Only the stair hall 401 reaches 2.67 m.

question: The original answer splits the Digital Hub's 2,842 m² of rooms into ad-hoc groups ("Other", "Circulation", "Office" …). Re-split the net floor area into the three DIN 277 categories. Then work out how much of it counts as lettable area under the German commercial letting guideline (GIF).
answer: Usable ≈ 1,555 m², technical function ≈ 367 m², traffic ≈ 920 m². Lettable area ≈ 2,331 m² (≈ 82 % of 2,842 m²). Under DIN 277 the net floor area is usable area + technical function area + traffic area. Usable area: offices, labs, seminar and conference rooms, cafeteria, kitchen and lounges (1,398.6 m²), plus WCs (93.6 m²) and stores/cleaning room (63.3 m²), giving 1,555.5 m². Technical function area: the plant rooms RLT-Raum, Hausanschluss, Wasser-/Gasverteilung, Heizzentrale, NSHV and BMZ (350.2 m²), plus the four accessible shafts (17.0 m²), giving 367.1 m². Traffic area: entrance hall and corridors (775.3 m²), stairwells and lift shafts (128.4 m²) and the two escape corridors (15.9 m²), giving 919.5 m². Under GIF, stairs, lifts, emergency exits, services rooms and shafts are not lettable. WCs and communal traffic areas (entrance halls, corridors) are lettable. Lettable area = 2,842.1 − (128.4 + 15.9 + 350.2 + 17.0) = 2,330.8 m². Assumptions: the "Fluchtflur" spaces count as emergency exits, the BMZ (fire-alarm control room) counts as a services room, and no room has a clear height of ≤ 1.50 m.

The following do not belong to the letting area: stairs, lifts, emergency exits, escape balconies, services rooms, shafts, protection rooms, areas of columns, pillars and separate walls, areas with a clear ceiling height of 1.50 m or less.

question: Fantasy office building 3 has occupied floors EG to OK OG4 (top floor at 14.80 m, storey height 3.70 m). Two stair cores sit at the south end (west and east). Each is reached from a 21.3 m corridor running north–south along the building edge. The owner wants to add two more identical office storeys. Would the existing floor layout then still meet the escape-route requirements? Check the corridor width, the corridor length, the length of corridor with only one escape direction, and the walking distance from the farthest point of "Open-plan office 1".
answer: No. Two extra storeys put the top floor at 14.80 + 2 × 3.70 = 22.20 m, which is more than 22 m, so the high-rise rules apply. (1) Width: the corridors are 1.51–1.58 m wide on the upper floors (1.66–1.73 m on EG), which meets the 1.25 m minimum. (2) Length: each corridor runs 21.28 m (y −20.80…0.48), within the 40 m maximum, but it exceeds 20 m, so a smoke-proof self-closing door would be needed. None is modelled. (3) Direction: each corridor leads only south to its own stair door (y ≈ −18.7 m). From its north end (y 0.48) that is ≈ 19 m with a single escape direction. Branch corridors may be at most 10 m (20 m with a second escape route such as an escape balcony), so this fails. (4) Walking distance: Open-plan office 1 (y 7.20–10.60) has no door to a corridor. Its occupants leave through Meeting room 2 and the Small office space, or through Meeting room 1 and the Kitchen. Measuring between door centres: ≈ 8.6 m to the open-plan door, + 1.1 m across the meeting room, + 6.4 m across the small office, + 19.4 m along the corridor, ≈ 35 m to the stairwell door. That is well over the 25 m limit (and already at the 35 m general limit). So the extension would need, for example, a third stair or escape stair at the north end, a corridor connection from the north offices, and smoke doors.
evidence: Storeys EG 0.00, OG1 3.70, OK OG2 7.40, OK OG3 11.10, OK OG4 14.80, OK OG5 18.50 m (roof); occupied spaces up to OK OG4.
Stair doors (EN 179) 31Jmzg6N54ZQqCBfl7HA5C (west, y −19.25…−18.20) and 31Jmzg6N54ZQqCBfl7HA5B (east, y −19.23…−18.18) on OG1; staircase cores at y −19.25…−13.78 m.

hidden_knowledge: High-rise when the top floor is > 22 m above ground; high-rise escape routes ≥ 1.25 m wide, walking distance ≤ 25 m, corridors ≤ 40 m with a smoke-proof door after 20 m, one-direction branch corridors ≤ 10 m (20 m with a second escape route).

basis.quote: High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.

Escape routes are min. 1.25 m wide and should if possible lead in two directions, to each staircase. The maximum walking distance from each point of an occupied room may not exceed 25 m. Corridors with two escape directions may be max. 40 m long. After 20 m, a smoke-proof self-closing door must be installed. Branch corridors with only one escape direction may be max. 10 m long. If a second escape route (e.g. an escape balcony) is available, max. 20 m.

question: The top floor of fantasy office building 1 (OG4) is at 19.20 m. If a sixth storey (OG5 at 24.00 m) were added on the two cross bars, the building would fall under the high-rise rules. Which of the existing glass façades would then fail the requirement against fire spreading from one storey to the next, and which could pass? Consider the long outer curtain walls of the wings, the storey-height curtain walls on the north and south bar façades, and the curtain walls on the inner (courtyard) faces of the wings at OG2–OG3.
answer: The uppermost floor would be at 24.0 m (> 22 m), so it becomes a high-rise. Each storey then needs a W 90 A parapet at least 1 m high (the fire-spread height), or a W 90 A horizontal element projecting at least 1.5 m. All-glass façades are allowed only with special approval and measures such as area sprinklers. (1) Long outer façades: fail. Curtain walls 2S7nIm7p… (x ≈ 10.0) and 0N9CSx…Ow$n (x ≈ −12.0) are single 2.4 × 2.4 m grid walls running unbroken from 0.00 to 18.79 m past every slab, i.e. all-glass façades. They would need special approval with sprinklers, or a 1.5 m projecting fire shelf at each floor. (2) Bar façades: can pass. Each storey has its own 3.50 m curtain wall starting at floor level (e.g. OG1 4.80–8.30, OG2 9.60–13.10, OG3 14.40–17.90 m). That leaves a 1.30 m opaque band (8.30 → 9.60 m) between one storey's glazing and the next. This meets the 1 m fire-spread height, provided the slab edge and spandrel are built W 90 A. (3) Courtyard faces of the wings at OG2/OG3: fail. The panels are 4.00 m high (9.60–13.60, 14.40–18.40 m), leaving only 0.80 m (13.60 → 14.40 m), which is less than 1 m. A W 90 A projection of at least 1.5 m, or lower glazing heads, would be needed.

In order to avoid fire spreading from one storey to the one above, there must be W 90 A fire-resistant parapets at least 1 m high (fire spreading height).
Alternatively, a W 90 A horizontal building element projecting at least 1.5 m from the façade can be provided.

question: On every floor of ac20, a pair of 1.80 m doors (Tür-017 and Tür-018) separates the central stair hall ("Flur … Treppe", 5.4 m wide, containing the building's only stair) from the two corridor wings, each 17.7 m long, which serve the offices and labs. What fire-safety purpose do these doors serve, what properties must they have, and would the corridor arrangement be acceptable without them?
answer: They divide the escape corridor and close off the stair. Without them, wing + hall + wing forms one continuous escape corridor of ≈ 41.4 m per floor: west wing x 0.30–18.00 (17.7 m), stair hall x 18.30–23.70 (5.4 m), east wing x 24.00–41.70 (17.7 m). Legally essential corridors longer than 30 m must be subdivided by self-closing, smoke-proof closures. Closures between a stairway and the escape corridors must also be self-closing and smoke-proof. Tür-017/018 do both jobs: they cut the corridor into segments of 17.7 m (< 30 m) and keep smoke from either wing out of the single stair, which is the only vertical escape route. Without them, the 41 m undivided corridor would open straight onto the stair, which is not acceptable. So the doors must be self-closing and smoke-proof.

Stairs Treppe-KG, Treppe-EG, Treppe-1-OG, Treppe-2-OG: one stair per floor, in the "Flur … Treppe" hall.

question: ac20 is an institute building. It has single and shared offices, student offices and laboratories on three floors, plus seminar, meeting and plant rooms in the basement and an attic. Going through the room schedule, which staff room required by workplace regulations is missing, and where could it be fitted without enlarging the building?
answer: A rest/break room is missing. Neufert states the rule in the staff area of its catering-kitchen section: for more than 10 employees a rest/break room is necessary (workplace regulations). Applying that workplace-regulation threshold to the institute's staff by analogy, ac20 clearly has more than 10 employees. The 1. OG alone has 17 offices, two of them named for two people (Buero Mueller VI + VII, VIII + IX), so at least 19 workplaces. The EG adds 8 single offices plus three student offices with 6–10 furniture units each, and the 2. OG adds 19 offices. Yet the schedule has no break, rest or tea room: besides offices there are only labs, WCs, corridors, two meeting rooms, a seminar room, plant rooms and the attic. A suitable place would be a daylit room of about 24–25 m² close to the central stair hall. Candidates are one of the 24.75 m² offices (e.g. 2. OG 302–306) or one of the basement meeting rooms (Besprechungsraum I/II, 23.9/24.8 m², with windows into the light wells). The attic (clear height ≤ 1.64 m) is unsuitable.

question: The basement "Seminarraum" (006) of ac20 measures about 11.6 × 11.4 m (128.3 m²) with a clear height of 2.70 m. Its sixteen 1.0 × 1.5 m windows open into light wells, eight on the south wall and eight on the north wall. By usual university seminar standards, for how many students is this room sized, and does that match the usual seminar room sizes? Is its depth acceptable for natural ventilation?
answer: It is sized for about 64–67 students, which is more than the usual seminar sizes. At 1.90–2.00 m² per student, 128.27 m² gives 128.27 / 2.00 ≈ 64 to 128.27 / 1.90 ≈ 67 students. The usual seminar sizes are 20, 40, 50 and 60 seats; the largest (60 seats) needs only ≈ 114–120 m². So this room is a small lecture room rather than a standard seminar room. Ventilation: with windows in one wall only, the room depth should not exceed 2.5 × clear height = 2.5 × 2.70 = 6.75 m. The 11.4 m depth would fail that. Here, though, the windows are in both long walls (y ≈ 2.2 and 13.8 m), so the room is cross-ventilated. Each façade serves about half the depth (≈ 5.7 m < 6.75 m), and the depth is acceptable. Closing either row of windows would make the room too deep.

The clear height is about 3.5 m. Which seat capacities was the designer evidently aiming at, and is the room depth adequate if the rooms are ventilated only through that façade?
answer: Standard 20- and 40-seat seminar rooms. At 1.90–2.00 m² per student, the large room (76.21 m²) holds ≈ 38–40 students, i.e. the 40-seat size. Each half after division (≈ 38 m², each served by its own door) holds ≈ 19–20. The single Seminarraum (37.69 m²) holds ≈ 19–20 as well. question: On the first floor of ac20, the institute head ("Buero IL", 36.7 m²) has an adjoining secretariat ("Buero IL Sekr.", 24.8 m², one workstation). Scientific staff sit in single offices of 11.1–12.0 m² ("Buero Mueller I–V", "Schmidt", "Schmid", "Schmied I/II", "Schmitt I/II") and in the two-person rooms "Buero Mueller VI + VII" and "VIII + IX" (24.8 m² each). question: The two precast half-turn stairs on the ground floor of the DigitalHub (Fertigbetontreppe:Treppe:2421059 in the west stairwell and :2423903 in the east stairwell, E00_OKRD to E01_OKRD) each have two straight runs and one intermediate landing slab. Judging from the model geometry, is the intermediate landing adequately sized for these flights? Compare with the assembled half-turn stair Zusammengebaute Treppe:Treppe:2424673 on the same floor.
answer: Yes, by the rules the book states. Landings are mandatory here, since the storey height is 3.90 m (E00 −0.15 m to E01 +3.75 m, 22 risers × 0.177 m), i.e. ≥2.75 m. The book's caption asks only that the landing width be ≥ the stair width: the landing slab spans 2.80 m across both runs (each ≈1.30 m wide, geometry bounding box, together x 14.13–16.93 m), so it is wider than either flight. The landing-length rule (n × stride + 1 tread = 2 × 0.177 + 0.27 = 0.624 m stride, + 0.27 = ≈0.89 m for n = 1) is also met by the ≈1.24 m depth (bbox 2.80 × 1.24 m). What the model does show is that this depth in the direction of travel is ≈6 cm less than the flight width (and smaller still if the ≈0.12 m by which the run bounding boxes reach into the landing were taken off). The caption does not say that the depth must equal the flight width, so this is not a breach of the stated rule; reading "width" as that depth would be an interpretation beyond the text. The assembled stair :2424673 (runs ≈1.30 m, landing ≈1.33 m deep, bbox 1.33 × 2.80 m) is the more generous design.

question: For an early cost estimate, the cost planner needs the net built volume of the DigitalHub basement level B01_OKRD (all twelve spaces, technical rooms, stores, corridor and both stairwells). Compute it from the model and say why simply multiplying the basement floor area by the storey height would give the wrong figure.
answer: ≈1,683 m³. The net built volume is the net floor area of each room times its clear ceiling height: the ten rooms with 3.00 m clear height (RLT-Raum 206.37, Flur-UG 105.04, Heizzentrale 53.97, five × 26.49, Putzmittel and BMZ 10.34 m² each = 518.52 m²) give 1,555.6 m³; the two stairwells (19.79 m² each, 3.22 m) give 127.4 m³. Total net floor area 558.1 m², net volume ≈1,683 m³. Multiplying by the storey height (B01 −3.37 m to E00 −0.15 m = 3.22 m) gives ≈1,797 m³, which mixes the net floor area with a floor-to-floor height. The floor-to-floor height belongs to the gross built volume, which multiplies the gross (outside-dimension) floor area by the height from top of floor covering to top of floor covering. The Qto Height of the spaces is taken here as the clear height.
